name: Degenerative (atraumatic) rotator cuff tear
populations: adults in their 50s and older (trial participants averaged 56–68 years)
people with repetitive overhead work or load
people with a partial-thickness tear or an existing tear on the other shoulder
many people with no symptoms at all
summary: A gradual, age-related failure of a cuff tendon, usually supraspinatus, without a clear injury. Tears are common in people with no pain, and many painful tears improve with exercise.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Pain and function often improve over months with an exercise program (timing is a clinical convention); the tear itself is not expected to heal

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based return to work and recreation; loaded overhead tasks commonly after about 3–6 months of progressive loading (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Lag signs for full-thickness tears (external rotation LR+ 7.2, internal rotation LR+ 5.6); painful arc (LR+ 3.7) for cuff disease in general

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound or MRI: sensitivity and specificity over 0.90 for full-thickness tears, but abnormalities are common in pain-free shoulders

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Cuff abnormality prevalence rises from 9.7% (aged 20 or younger) to 62% (aged 80 or older), with or without symptoms

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Full-thickness tears on ultrasound in 11–17% of two population-based samples of asymptomatic shoulders (low-certainty evidence)

overview:
A degenerative (atraumatic) rotator cuff tear is a partial- or full-thickness failure of a cuff tendon, most often supraspinatus, that develops gradually without a clear injury. It is largely a condition of ageing. In a pooled analysis of 30 studies (6112 shoulders), the prevalence of cuff abnormalities rose from 9.7% in people aged 20 years or younger to 62% in those aged 80 or older, and the rise was similar whether or not people had symptoms, which makes it difficult to know whether an abnormality on imaging is the cause of pain [r1]. A systematic review of asymptomatic shoulders found full-thickness tears on ultrasound in 11% to 17% in two population-based samples (1631 shoulders), but the overall range for imaging abnormalities was 0% to 100% and the certainty of evidence was low to very low [r2]. The presence of a tear on a scan should therefore never be treated as proof that it is the source of the patient's pain.

For people with a symptomatic tear, exercise is a reasonable first-line option for many. In a three-arm trial of 180 shoulders with symptomatic, nontraumatic supraspinatus tears in people older than 55 years, physiotherapy alone, acromioplasty plus physiotherapy, and repair plus acromioplasty plus physiotherapy produced similar changes in Constant score at two years (18.4, 20.5 and 22.6 points) [r3]. At a mean of 6.2 years (mean age 71 years), the changes were still similar (18.5, 17.9 and 20.0 points), although 8 shoulders in the physiotherapy-only group had crossed over to repair [r4]. A Cochrane review of nine trials found moderate-certainty evidence that surgery probably provides little or no improvement in pain at one year compared with non-operative care (0.87 points better on a 0–10 scale), and low-certainty evidence of a 6-point difference in function on a 0–100 scale. The authors cautioned that the trials mostly included small degenerative supraspinatus tears, so the findings may not apply to traumatic tears, large tears involving subscapularis, or young people [r5].

Longer-term evidence is less settled. In a randomised trial of 103 patients with full-thickness tears not exceeding 3 cm, results at 15 years favoured primary tendon repair (Constant score 11.8 points higher and pain 1.8 cm lower on a 10-cm scale), 15 of 51 patients in the physiotherapy group had crossed over to surgery, and unrepaired tears had enlarged [r6]. For large to massive tears, a meta-analysis of five trials (297 participants) found low or very low certainty evidence, with a small pain advantage for surgery at 12 months (0.47 points) and a small advantage in external rotation range for exercise [r7]. A clinical practice guideline advises an active, task-oriented rehabilitation program for adults with cuff disorders and considers surgery appropriate for selected patients with a full-thickness tear [r8]. Lewis concluded that graduated exercise confers at least equivalent benefit to surgery for atraumatic full-thickness tears, while noting that outcomes may be incomplete, with persisting or recurring symptoms [r9]. The practical message is shared decision-making, a trial of structured exercise for many people, and monitoring for tear progression.

epidemiology.text: Cuff abnormalities become more common with each decade of life and are common in people with no symptoms. In a pooled analysis of 30 studies (6112 shoulders), prevalence rose from 9.7% (29 of 299) in people aged 20 years or younger to 62% (166 of 268) in people aged 80 or older, with a similar increase regardless of symptoms; the authors concluded that cuff degeneration is a common aspect of normal ageing [r1]. In asymptomatic shoulders, full-thickness tears on ultrasound were found in 11% to 17% in two population-based samples (1631 shoulders), 0% to 35% across 14 studies of miscellaneous populations, and 0% to 22% across four studies of athletes, although the certainty of this evidence was low to very low [r2]. The participants in trials of exercise versus surgery for degenerative tears had mean ages of 56 to 68 years, 29% to 56% were female, and symptom duration averaged 10 to 28 months [r5]. A narrative review lists several factors associated with cuff tears, including age, a history of trauma, limb dominance, a tear in the contralateral shoulder, smoking, hypercholesterolaemia, posture and occupational demands; these are associations, and causation has not been established [r10].

intrinsic: Increasing age: prevalence of cuff abnormality rises steadily from the third decade, with or without symptoms [r1]
A tear in the other shoulder, and limb dominance (associated factors in a narrative review) [r10]
Smoking and hypercholesterolaemia (associated factors; modifiable, but a causal effect on the cuff has not been shown) [r10]
A partial-thickness tear or an existing small tear, which can enlarge over time (see pathophysiology)
extrinsic: Occupational demands and posture (associated factors; narrative review) [r10]
A previous history of trauma to the shoulder [r10]
Repetitive overhead or heavy loading (a plausible contributor in the continuum model, but trial evidence is limited)
Prolonged unloading or deconditioning of the cuff (clinical reasoning; not established)

mechanism.summary: A degenerative tear has no single injury. It is thought to arise from cumulative tendon pathology in which load repeatedly exceeds the capacity of an ageing tendon, so that regions of disorganised matrix develop and eventually fail, usually near the supraspinatus footprint. Intrinsic (age-related) and extrinsic (load, subacromial) contributors are both proposed, and no single model explains all presentations [r11,r12].
sequence: Repeated or sustained load, often overhead or away from the body, is placed on a cuff tendon whose capacity has fallen with age.
Tendon cells respond to the overload by changing matrix production: this is the reactive stage of the continuum model, which can still recover [r11,r12].
With continued load, matrix disorganisation increases. Disorganised regions become unable to transmit tensile load and may overload adjacent tendon that still looks normal [r12].
A partial-thickness tear develops, commonly in supraspinatus near its footprint on the greater tuberosity (clinical convention).
In some people the tear enlarges over months to years, from partial to full thickness and from supraspinatus into neighbouring tendons.
The muscle atrophies and accumulates fat, and in large tears the humeral head can migrate superiorly.
A minor event such as reaching or lifting often makes the tear symptomatic, although the tear was already present.

variants.name: Incidental (asymptomatic) tear
variants.description: A tear found on imaging in a person with no pain, very common with increasing age [r1,r2]. Management is usually no tendon-directed treatment.

variants.name: Symptomatic partial-thickness tear
variants.description: Bursal-sided, articular-sided or intratendinous. Partial tears can enlarge and progress to full-thickness tears with time [r10].

variants.name: Small-to-medium full-thickness supraspinatus tear
variants.description: The population in most exercise-versus-surgery trials: mostly small degenerative supraspinatus tears, with tears involving subscapularis often excluded [r5].

variants.name: Large to massive tear
variants.description: More than 5 cm or involving two or more tendons [r7]. Higher risk of fatty infiltration and loss of the force couple; evidence for exercise versus surgery is of low to very low certainty [r7].

variants.name: Reactive-on-degenerative flare
variants.description: A structurally degenerate tendon enters a painful reactive phase after a spike in load; the normal portion of the tendon can drift in and out of a reactive response [r12].

variants.name: Acute-on-chronic extension
variants.description: A previously quiet degenerate tear is extended by a fall or sudden pull, with sudden weakness. Assess as an acute tear (see traumatic rotator cuff tear).

anatomy.text: The rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis) forms a tendinous sleeve around the humeral head that compresses and centres the head in the glenoid during elevation, balancing the upward pull of the deltoid. The supraspinatus tendon passes beneath the acromion and coracoacromial ligament, separated from them by the subacromial–subdeltoid bursa, and inserts on the greater tuberosity. The area just proximal to this footprint, often called the critical zone, is a common site of tear initiation. The long head of biceps runs through the rotator interval between supraspinatus and subscapularis. Cuff tendon failure alters the balance of these forces and, if large, allows the humeral head to rise toward the acromion.

structures.name: Supraspinatus tendon and footprint
structures.role: Abduction and humeral head compression; the most commonly affected tendon in degenerative tear trials [r5]

structures.name: Infraspinatus and teres minor
structures.role: External rotation and posterior stability; involved as tears extend posteriorly

structures.name: Subscapularis
structures.role: Internal rotation and anterior stability; often excluded from trial populations [r5]

structures.name: Long head of biceps tendon and rotator interval
structures.role: Passes between supraspinatus and subscapularis; a path for tear extension and a possible pain source

structures.name: Acromion, coracoacromial ligament and subacromial bursa
structures.role: The roof and gliding surface above the tendon, where contact and bursal irritation are proposed contributors to pain

structures.name: Greater tuberosity
structures.role: Footprint of supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
The continuum model of tendon pathology proposes that overloaded tendon moves from a reactive stage (tenocyte activation, proteoglycan expression and changes in collagen type) through disrepair to a degenerative stage in which regions of disorganised matrix cannot transmit tensile load. The model was developed from lower limb tendons and has been adapted for the rotator cuff. It is a structural model: it does not propose a direct relationship between structure, pain and dysfunction, and degenerative regions appear to have limited reversibility, so treatment aims to build load capacity in the aligned tissue rather than to regenerate the disorganised region [r11,r12]. Structural pathology is better regarded as a risk factor for symptoms, and progression over time may be a greater risk factor for pain than the absolute extent of pathology [r12].

Non-operatively treated tears can enlarge, and the risk differs by tear type. In an MRI study of 59 shoulders (mean age 58.8 years) monitored for at least six months, tears progressed in 48% of shoulders followed for more than 18 months versus 19% followed for less, in 52% of full-thickness versus 8% of partial-thickness tears, and in 54% of patients over 60 versus 17% of those aged 60 or under; 24% of full-thickness tears had supraspinatus atrophy and fatty infiltration was associated with progression [r13]. In 122 patients followed for a mean of 24.4 months, tear size increased in 41.8% overall, in 82.4% (28 of 34) of full-thickness and 26.1% (23 of 88) of partial-thickness tears, and full-thickness tear was the most reliable risk factor for enlargement [r14]. A pooled estimate from four studies (257 tears) put the rate of progression from partial- to full-thickness tear at 0.26% per month, with no significant difference between symptomatic and asymptomatic tears [r15]. A review of 21 articles (1831 tears) found a progression rate of 26.7% for partial-thickness tears at an average of 2.2 years and 54.9% for full-thickness tears at 3.0 years, but used 5 and 8 different definitions of progression, and tears that became symptomatic progressed more often (33%–63%) than tears that stayed asymptomatic (4%–38%) [r16]. In 79 shoulders with symptomatic tears managed non-operatively, a mediolateral tear size of 20 mm or more at baseline was associated with relevant progression of supraspinatus fatty infiltration (odds ratio 19.0) [r17].

structures.name: Supraspinatus tendon (footprint and critical zone)
structures.effect: Matrix disorganisation, then partial- and full-thickness tearing; the usual site in degenerative tear trials [r5]

structures.name: Infraspinatus and subscapularis tendons
structures.effect: Involved as tears extend; multi-tendon tears carry a worse structural outlook (large to massive tears) [r7]

structures.name: Long head of biceps tendon and rotator interval
structures.effect: Can be affected by tear extension and may contribute to anterior pain (proposed)

structures.name: Subacromial–subdeltoid bursa
structures.effect: Bursal-sided partial tears and bursal inflammation are possible pain contributors (proposed)

structures.name: Glenohumeral joint
structures.effect: Over years, large tears can lead to cuff tear arthropathy [r10]; glenohumeral osteoarthritis progressed in the trial population over 6.2 years whether or not the tear was repaired [r4]

muscles.name: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus
muscles.effect: Atrophy (24% of full-thickness tears versus none of the partial-thickness tears in one MRI study) and fatty infiltration, which is associated with tear progression [r13,r17]; loss of strength reflects both pain inhibition and loss of force transmission through the torn tendon (proposed)

muscles.name: Deltoid and upper trapezius
muscles.effect: Compensatory overactivity and shoulder hitching on elevation (clinical observation)

muscles.name: Scapular stabilisers
muscles.effect: Altered recruitment with pain and weakness; tendinopathy is associated with reduced muscle strength and motor control [r12]

muscles.name: Subscapularis and teres minor
muscles.effect: Assessed separately; subscapularis involvement changes the prognosis and surgical options [r5]

cellular.description: Tenocytes respond to overload with cell activation, proteoglycan expression and changes in collagen type. The tendon thickens and can regain normal structure with optimal management [r11,r12].
Matrix breakdown and disorganisation increase, with an attempted but inadequate repair response [r11].
Regions of disorganised matrix become mechanically silent and unable to transmit load, with a persistent hyperactive tenocyte response and limited reversibility [r12].
Partial-thickness tears may enlarge and progress to full thickness; progression rates differ by tear type and by how progression is defined [r13,r14,r15,r16].
Atrophy and fatty infiltration of the torn muscle, associated with progression and with a worse treatment outcome [r13,r17].

systems.effect: Pain does not track structure: the same tear can be painless or painful, and the nociceptive driver in tendon pain remains uncertain; sensitisation and altered motor control are described [r12]
Cuff degeneration is common in normal ageing [r1]; smoking and hypercholesterolaemia are associated factors, although causation is not shown [r10]
Large tears reduce the cuff's ability to centre the head; the scapula compensates by hitching, and in the long term cuff tear arthropathy can develop [r10]
Being told of a 'tear' can increase fear of movement and avoidance; sleep disturbance from night pain amplifies pain (clinical observation)
Reduced tendon blood supply with age and in the critical zone is often proposed as a contributor to degeneration, but this was not examined in the sources reviewed here

grading.system: Descriptive classification by thickness, size and muscle quality (no single universally accepted system)

grades.description: Bursal-sided, articular-sided or intratendinous tear that does not pass completely through the tendon [r10].
grades.prognosis: In non-operatively treated tears, 8% of partial-thickness tears increased in size in one MRI study, versus 52% of full-thickness tears [r13]; a pooled estimate for progression to full thickness was 0.26% per month [r15].

grades.grade: Full-thickness, small to medium (up to about 3 cm)
grades.description: Complete tear through the tendon thickness, usually isolated supraspinatus. The long-term trial of repair versus physiotherapy enrolled full-thickness tears not exceeding 3 cm [r6]; in the Finnish trial the mean sagittal tear size at baseline was 10 mm [r4].
grades.prognosis: Exercise outcomes were similar to surgery at 2 and 6.2 years in the Finnish trials [r3,r4], whereas the Norwegian trial favoured repair at 15 years [r6]; the evidence is conflicting.

grades.description: Larger tears often involving more than one tendon (conventional size band; trials do not define it separately).
grades.prognosis: Tear size of 20 mm or more at baseline was associated with relevant fatty infiltration progression in one MRI cohort [r17]. Early orthopaedic review is reasonable.

grades.grade: Massive (more than 5 cm or two or more tendons)
grades.description: The definition used in a meta-analysis of large to massive tears [r7].
grades.prognosis: Low to very low certainty evidence for exercise versus surgery: pain favoured surgery by 0.47 points at 12 months and external rotation range favoured exercise [r7].

grades.grade: Muscle quality modifier (fatty infiltration and atrophy)
grades.description: Graded separately from tear size, for example by Goutallier grade or quantitative fat fraction on MRI [r17].
grades.prognosis: Fatty infiltration was associated with tear progression [r13,r17].

timeframes.summary: A degenerative tear does not heal like an acute injury, so the timeline describes symptom settling and capacity building rather than tissue repair. Unrepaired tears may enlarge over years even while symptoms improve [r6,r13,r14]. The phases below are typical clinical ranges, not trial-derived.

healing.description: Education, load modification, pain-guided isometrics and range of motion (clinical convention). Heavy provocative loading is avoided in an irritable (reactive) tendon [r12].

Progressive isotonic loading of the cuff and scapular muscles, with pain-guided progression. Treatment targets capacity in the aligned tendon and muscle rather than regeneration of the disorganised region [r12].

healing.phase: Strengthen, return to function and monitor
healing.description: Heavier and task-specific loading, with review for tear progression if symptoms or strength worsen, particularly for full-thickness tears [r13,r14].

milestones.label: Review response to exercise
milestones.note: Clinical convention: if no improvement after about 12 weeks of well-delivered loading, reconsider diagnosis, imaging and a surgical opinion

milestones.label: Strength re-test against the other side
Annual review for progression if full-thickness
milestones.note: Full-thickness tears progressed more often than partial tears [r13,r14]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based return to work and recreation, not time-based. Loaded overhead tasks commonly follow about 3–6 months of progressive loading (clinical convention). If surgery is chosen, follow the surgeon's protocol, which is a separate pathway.

symptoms: Gradual onset of lateral shoulder or upper arm pain, worse with overhead or loaded reaching
Night pain and difficulty lying on the affected side
Weakness or fatigue when lifting the arm, often noticed with a minor trigger such as reaching or lifting
Pain with dressing, reaching behind the back or carrying
Sometimes no pain at all: many tears are found incidentally [r1,r2]
Stiffness is not typical early; marked stiffness suggests a different diagnosis such as frozen shoulder
signs: Weakness of resisted external rotation and abduction, which may be pain-limited or true weakness
External or internal rotation lag signs, or a positive drop-arm test, in larger full-thickness tears [r18]
Passive range largely preserved (unless stiffness coexists)
Shoulder hitching and compensatory trunk lean on elevation
Later or in large tears: wasting of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossae and superior head migration

subjective: Onset: gradual or insidious versus a clear injury (a fall or sudden pull suggests an acute or acute-on-chronic tear)
Behaviour of pain: load-related, night pain, and what the person can and cannot do (dressing, overhead work, sleep)
Previous shoulder pain, injections, imaging reports and any tear on the other side
Age, hand dominance, occupation, recreation and goals, because they shape the choice between exercise and surgery
Medical history relevant to risk and healing: smoking, lipids, diabetes and medications [r10]
Beliefs and fears about the tear, sleep, mood, and previous response to exercise
Red-flag screen: unexplained weight loss, fever, night pain unrelated to movement, chest symptoms, neurological symptoms
observation: Wasting of supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossae (more likely in larger or longer-standing tears)
Scapular position and shoulder hitching during elevation
Posture and willingness to elevate the arm
Bruising, swelling or deformity, which would suggest an acute injury rather than a degenerative tear
palpation: Greater tuberosity and anterior acromion (supraspinatus footprint area)
Bicipital groove (long head of biceps) and anterior shoulder (subscapularis)
AC joint and cervical spine as alternative pain sources
rangeOfMotion: Active elevation, external rotation and internal rotation compared with passive range; a large active deficit with full passive range suggests tendon failure or weakness
Passive range of motion: usually preserved; a global loss of passive external rotation points toward frozen shoulder
strength: Resisted external rotation at the side and abduction in the scapular plane, noting pain versus true weakness; a positive external rotation resistance test was among the most accurate findings for cuff disease in general [r18]
External rotation lag sign and internal rotation lag sign for full-thickness tears [r18]
Belly-press, belly-off and lift-off tests for subscapularis (accuracy figures not taken from the sources reviewed here)
Hand-held dynamometry of external rotation and abduction as a baseline for monitoring
neuro: Cervical screen: neck movement, Spurling test and upper limb neurodynamic tests, since cervical radiculopathy can mimic shoulder pain
Dermatomes, myotomes and reflexes of the upper limb
Suprascapular nerve: wasting and external rotation weakness without a lag sign
Axillary nerve function (deltoid contraction, lateral shoulder sensation) if there has been trauma
functional: Ability to elevate actively against gravity and hold the arm at 90°
Hand-behind-back, overhead reach and work-specific tasks

specialTests.name: External rotation lag sign
specialTests.procedure: Passively hold the arm in near-maximal external rotation with the elbow flexed at the side (or in the scapular plane) and ask the patient to maintain the position as you release the wrist.
specialTests.positive: The arm drifts into internal rotation (a lag).

specialTests.name: Internal rotation lag sign
specialTests.purpose: Full-thickness tear (classically used for subscapularis); a normal result helps to exclude a full-thickness tear
specialTests.procedure: Place the hand behind the back with the hand lifted off the back by the examiner, then ask the patient to hold it there as you release.
specialTests.positive: The hand falls back onto the back instead of staying lifted.

specialTests.name: Drop-arm test
specialTests.procedure: Passively abduct the arm to 90° and ask the patient to lower it slowly.
specialTests.positive: The arm drops or cannot be lowered smoothly.

specialTests.name: Painful arc test
specialTests.purpose: Cuff disease in general (not specific to a tear)
specialTests.procedure: Active elevation through abduction or the scapular plane, observing for pain in mid-range.
specialTests.positive: Pain through the mid-range of elevation that eases above and below.

specialTests.name: External rotation resistance test
specialTests.procedure: With the elbows at the side and flexed to 90°, resist isometric external rotation and compare sides for pain and weakness.
specialTests.positive: Pain or weakness compared with the other side. A positive result was among the most accurate findings for cuff disease, although no figure is quoted here.

clinicalRules.name: A tear on imaging is not the same as a painful tear
clinicalRules.description: Cuff abnormality is common in people with no symptoms and increases with age [r1,r2]. Interpret imaging against the history and examination, and avoid telling patients that a tear explains their pain unless the clinical picture agrees.

clinicalRules.name: Lag signs identify tears, painful arc identifies cuff disease
clinicalRules.description: Lag signs were the most accurate findings for a full-thickness tear, whereas painful arc and external rotation resistance were most accurate for cuff disease in general. All tests were performed by specialists in referred patients, so generalisability to a non-referred population is unknown [r18].

clinicalRules.name: Sudden weakness changes the pathway
clinicalRules.description: A sudden loss of strength after a fall or pull suggests an acute or acute-on-chronic tear, which is assessed more urgently (see traumatic rotator cuff tear).

outcomeMeasures.name: Constant–Murley score
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome in the trials of exercise versus surgery [r3,r4,r6]

outcomeMeasures.name: American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score
outcomeMeasures.use: Self-reported function, reported as a secondary outcome in the 15-year trial [r6]

outcomeMeasures.name: Visual analogue or numeric pain scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain at rest, at night and with activity; reported in the trials [r3,r6]

outcomeMeasures.name: Oxford Shoulder Score, SPADI or QuickDASH
outcomeMeasures.use: Patient-reported pain and function for routine monitoring

outcomeMeasures.name: Hand-held dynamometry (external rotation, abduction)
outcomeMeasures.use: Strength and limb symmetry; baseline for monitoring progression

imaging.indication: When a full-thickness tear would change management, or to monitor tear progression; point-of-care and low cost. A guideline advises that imaging is only necessary in select circumstances [r8]
imaging.findings: Sensitivity and specificity over 0.90 for full-thickness tears, and accuracy was similar whether a radiologist, sonographer or orthopaedist performed it [r19]

imaging.indication: Surgical planning, large or multi-tendon tears, or suspected muscle atrophy
imaging.findings: Sensitivity and specificity over 0.90 for full-thickness tears; for partial tears and tendinopathy specificity over 0.90 and sensitivity 0.67–0.83 [r19]. Fatty infiltration and tear size predict progression [r13,r17].

imaging.indication: Persistent pain, suspected arthritis, or large tears
imaging.findings: Superior head migration, glenohumeral osteoarthritis and cuff tear arthropathy in long-standing large tears [r10]; calcific deposits (see calcific tendinopathy)

differentials.name: Rotator cuff related shoulder pain
differentials.distinguishing: Overlapping spectrum: painful arc and pain-limited weakness without a lag sign; tendon-directed management is similar [r9].

differentials.name: Traumatic rotator cuff tear
differentials.distinguishing: A clear injury (fall, forceful pull) with sudden weakness; assessed more urgently than a degenerative tear.

differentials.name: Calcific tendinopathy of the rotator cuff
differentials.distinguishing: Often severe pain of rapid onset with a visible calcific deposit on radiograph or ultrasound, in a mid-life patient.

differentials.name: Frozen shoulder
differentials.distinguishing: Global loss of active and passive range, especially external rotation, rather than pain-limited weakness with preserved passive motion.

differentials.name: Long head of biceps tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Anterior pain over the bicipital groove with positive biceps loading tests; may coexist with a cuff tear.

differentials.name: Cervical radiculopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Neck-related pain with dermatomal symptoms, myotomal weakness and neck movements that reproduce the arm pain.

differentials.name: Acromioclavicular joint pain
differentials.distinguishing: Localised tenderness over the AC joint and pain on cross-body adduction rather than a mid-range painful arc.

differentials.name: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis or cuff tear arthropathy
differentials.distinguishing: Pain with crepitus, global stiffness and loss of joint space or head migration on radiograph [r10].

redFlags: Sudden loss of strength or inability to lift the arm after a fall or pull, with a lag or drop-arm sign: possible acute full-thickness tear. Arrange early imaging and an orthopaedic opinion rather than a long exercise trial.
Unremitting night or rest pain, unexplained weight loss, a history of cancer or systemic illness: consider malignancy or referred pain. Refer for medical assessment and imaging.
Fever, a hot, red, swollen shoulder, or recent injection or surgery: possible septic arthritis. Same-day medical review.
Arm weakness with dermatomal or myotomal loss, neck pain, or bilateral symptoms: consider cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy; refer for spinal assessment.
Chest pain or pressure, breathlessness or sweating with shoulder pain: possible cardiac cause. Seek emergency assessment.

Progressive weakness with an inability to elevate the arm despite passive range (pseudoparalysis) or marked muscle wasting: early orthopaedic referral, because large tears with atrophy and fatty infiltration are harder to treat [r13,r17].
Symptoms worsening or strength falling on a well-delivered program: re-image, since full-thickness tears can enlarge [r13,r14].

management.principles: Start by deciding whether the tear is likely to be relevant. Because cuff abnormalities are common in people without symptoms [r1,r2], the history and examination, not the scan, should drive decisions. For most people with a gradual-onset symptomatic tear, structured exercise with education is a reasonable first step: a guideline recommends an active, task-oriented rehabilitation program for cuff disorders [r8], a Cochrane review found that surgery probably gives little or no extra pain benefit at one year [r5], and trials in older adults with small supraspinatus tears showed similar outcomes at two and 6.2 years [r3,r4]. The evidence is not one-sided: the 15-year follow-up of a trial in full-thickness tears up to 3 cm favoured primary repair and found that unrepaired tears enlarged [r6], and evidence for large to massive tears is low to very low certainty [r7]. Surgery is considered appropriate for selected patients with a full-thickness tear [r8]. Share these uncertainties with the patient, tailor the decision to age, demand, tear size, muscle quality and goals, and monitor full-thickness tears for progression [r13,r14]. Load management and progressive loading apply whichever pathway is chosen.

medical.name: Selective imaging (ultrasound or MRI)
medical.description: Image when a full-thickness tear would change management: sudden weakness, an acute-on-chronic event, failure to improve, or surgical planning. A guideline advises that imaging is only necessary in select circumstances [r8]. Ultrasound has sensitivity and specificity over 0.90 for full-thickness tears [r19]. Interpret findings cautiously because abnormalities are common in pain-free shoulders [r1,r2].

medical.name: Short-term analgesia (paracetamol, NSAIDs)
medical.description: A guideline states that acetaminophen (paracetamol) and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs may be useful to reduce pain in the short term [r8]. Use the lowest effective dose and consider comorbidities. Analgesia supports, rather than replaces, loading.

medical.name: Subacromial or other corticosteroid injection
medical.description: The guideline states that injection therapies may be useful to reduce pain in the short term [r8], and one of the three trials in the Cochrane comparison provided up to three glucocorticoid injections in the exercise group [r5]. Injections do not address tendon capacity, and no source reviewed here showed a lasting structural benefit.

medical.name: Surgical repair (arthroscopic or open) for selected patients
medical.description: In small degenerative supraspinatus tears, trials found no significant difference in Constant score change between repair and physiotherapy at 2 years (22.6 versus 18.4) [r3] and at a mean of 6.2 years (20.0 versus 18.5) [r4]; the Cochrane review found moderate-certainty evidence of little or no pain benefit at one year [r5]. In contrast, the 15-year follow-up of a trial of full-thickness tears up to 3 cm favoured repair (Constant 11.8 points, ASES 13.9 points), and 15 of 51 patients in the physiotherapy arm had crossed over to surgery [r6]. A guideline considers surgery appropriate for selected patients with a full-thickness tear [r8]. Candidates include younger or high-demand people, larger or enlarging tears, acute-on-chronic tears, and people who fail a well-delivered exercise program.

medical.name: Subacromial decompression (acromioplasty) as an add-on
medical.description: In the Finnish trial, adding acromioplasty to physiotherapy did not change outcomes at two years (Constant score change 20.5 versus 18.4 points) [r3], and the guideline does not recommend subacromial decompression for rotator cuff tendinopathy [r8]. It should not be offered to improve pain in a degenerative tear.

physio.name: Progressive, task-oriented exercise program with education
physio.description: A guideline advises an active, task-oriented rehabilitation program (exercises and education) to reduce pain and disability in adults with cuff disorders [r8]. Lewis concluded that graduated, well-constructed exercise confers at least equivalent benefit to surgery for atraumatic full-thickness tears, with the caveat that outcomes may be incomplete and symptoms may persist or recur [r9]. In the trials, physiotherapy-only groups improved by about 18 Constant points at two years [r3] and at 6.2 years [r4]. In trials of large to massive tears, exercise interventions were poorly reported, so the optimal dosage is unknown [r7].

physio.name: Pain-guided loading targeted at capacity, not at the tear
physio.description: In the continuum model, degenerative regions have limited reversibility, so treatment aims to build load capacity in the aligned tendon and muscle (the 'doughnut', not the 'hole') through progressive loading [r12]. This model was developed in other tendons; cuff-specific evidence for it is limited.

physio.name: Education, reassurance and load management
physio.description: Explain that tears are common with age and often painless [r1,r2], that pain and tear size correlate poorly [r12], and that function can improve while the tear remains. Adjust the load, not necessarily stop it, and address sleep and fear of movement. Education is part of the guideline's recommended program [r8].

physio.name: Monitoring for progression
physio.description: Review strength and symptoms regularly. Full-thickness tears, tears in people over 60, larger tears and fatty infiltration are linked with enlargement or progression [r13,r14,r17], and re-imaging is reasonable if function declines. Definitions of progression vary widely between studies [r16].

physio.name: Heavy eccentric or provocative loading in an irritable (reactive) tendon
physio.description: In the continuum model, heavy eccentric loading may be highly provocative and deleterious during the reactive stage [r12]. Start with pain-guided isometrics and light isotonic work and progress as irritability settles. This is based on tendinopathy models more generally, not on a cuff trial.

physio.name: Passive, pain-only treatment as the sole intervention
physio.description: Interventions directed solely at pain have a minimal effect on strength deficits and load capacity and may result in recurrence of pain [r12]. Passive modalities can ease symptoms to allow loading but should not replace a loading program.

education: Rotator cuff tears are very common as we age, even in people with no pain. A tear on a scan does not always mean it is the cause of your pain.
Many painful degenerative tears improve with a progressive exercise program, and in trials of older adults with small tears outcomes were similar to surgery over several years.
Surgery is still a reasonable option for some people, particularly with larger, enlarging or persistently painful tears. We will review your progress and decide together.
Exercise should be challenging but tolerable. A pain level of up to about 3–4 out of 10 that settles within 24 hours is generally acceptable (a clinical convention).
Strength and comfort usually improve over weeks to months. The tear itself may not change, and some tears enlarge over time, so check in if your strength falls.
Seek urgent advice for a sudden loss of strength, new numbness, fever or a hot swollen shoulder.

rehab.overview: This is a non-operative, criteria-based progression. Dosages are common clinical conventions and not trial-derived prescriptions, because exercise interventions were poorly reported in the trials of large to massive tears, and optimal dosage is unknown [r7]. Progress when criteria are met, not on a calendar. Pain during exercise of up to about 3–4/10 that settles within 24 hours is acceptable (clinical convention). If surgery is chosen, the surgeon's protocol replaces this program.

stages.name: Settle and keep moving
goals: Maintain shoulder range and general activity
Educate about tears, pain and load
precautions: Avoid heavy or sustained loading overhead and away from the body while irritable
Do not provoke pain above about 4/10 or pain that is still elevated the next morning
Report sudden weakness, new numbness or fever

exercises.name: Pendulum swings
exercises.cues: Let the arm hang and swing from the trunk, shoulder relaxed

exercises.name: Supported or assisted elevation (supine or with the other hand)
exercises.cues: Lead with the other hand; stop at the first firm resistance

exercises.name: Isometric external rotation at the side
exercises.dosage: 5 × 30–45 s at about 30–50% effort, 1–2 times daily
exercises.cues: Elbow bent and tucked, press the back of the hand into a wall

exercises.name: Isometric abduction in the scapular plane
exercises.dosage: 5 × 30–45 s at about 30–50% effort, 1–2 times daily
exercises.cues: Press the elbow outwards into a wall, no shrug

exercises.name: Scapular setting and posture
exercises.cues: Gently draw the shoulder blades back and down

progressionCriteria: Isometric loading tolerated with pain ≤ 4/10 that settles within 24 hours
Active elevation to at least 90° with pain controlled

stages.name: Load and rebuild capacity
goals: Introduce progressive isotonic loading of the cuff and scapular muscles
precautions: Increase load or range one variable at a time
Avoid fast, heavy overhead lifting until strength and control improve

exercises.name: Band external rotation at the side
exercises.cues: Elbow tucked, keep the shoulder blade set

exercises.name: Side-lying external rotation
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–15 with a light dumbbell, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Elbow on the side, 2–3 s lowering

exercises.name: Scaption raise to about 60–90° (light)
exercises.cues: Thumb up, raise in the plane of the scapula, avoid shrugging

exercises.name: Row (band or dumbbell)
exercises.cues: Draw the shoulder blades back and down

exercises.name: Wall slide
exercises.cues: Keep the forearms on the wall and the shoulder blade moving

progressionCriteria: Active elevation to near full range without hitching
Pain ≤ 3/10 with exercise and daily tasks
Completes 3 × 12 of the band or light dumbbell exercises with good control

stages.name: Progressive strengthening
goals: Build cuff, deltoid and scapular strength and endurance
Return to heavier daily and work tasks
precautions: Increase load gradually (about 5–10% per week; clinical convention)
Monitor for a pain flare over 24 hours and reduce the load if it persists

exercises.name: Heavier scaption and flexion raise
exercises.dosage: 3–4 × 8–12, 2–3 times per week, progress the load as tolerated

exercises.name: Row progression
exercises.cues: Pause at the end of the pull

exercises.name: Incline or wall push-up plus
exercises.cues: Push through the hands and protract at the top

exercises.name: Prone Y raise
exercises.cues: Lift with the lower trapezius, not the neck

exercises.name: Light overhead press
exercises.cues: Press in the scapular plane with a stable trunk

progressionCriteria: Strength about 80% or more of the other side for external rotation and abduction (dynamometry)
Pain ≤ 2/10 with daily and light work tasks
Active elevation full or near full without hitching

stages.name: Return to full function and maintain
goals: Return to heavy or overhead work and recreation
precautions: Re-assess promptly if strength drops or a sudden weakness event occurs

exercises.name: Overhead press progression
exercises.cues: Press in the scapular plane, control the lowering

exercises.name: Push-up progression
exercises.cues: Straight trunk, protract at the top

exercises.name: Task or recreation-specific overhead drills (painting, racquet sport, lifting)
exercises.dosage: Start at about 30% of normal volume and build over 4–8 weeks (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Quality first, then volume, then intensity

progressionCriteria: Passes the strength, range and function criteria (see return to sport)
Completes work or recreation tasks at full volume with pain ≤ 2/10
Independent with a maintenance loading program (2 sessions per week, clinical convention)

criteria: Pain ≤ 2/10 with work or recreational tasks and no significant night pain
Full or near-full active range, equal to the other side, without hitching
External rotation and abduction strength about 90% or more of the other side (clinical convention)
No new lag signs, and good scapular control during loaded elevation
Completes task or sport-specific training at full volume without symptoms
Understands the monitoring plan and maintenance program
Time: loaded overhead tasks commonly after about 3–6 months of progressive loading (clinical convention)
tests: Hand-held dynamometry for external rotation and abduction compared with the other side
External and internal rotation lag signs at final assessment
Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test
Overhead endurance and task simulation (work or sport specific)
Constant score, Oxford Shoulder Score or SPADI at baseline and return

prognosis: Most people with a symptomatic degenerative tear improve with exercise, but the structural outlook is different from the clinical one. In the Finnish trial, Constant score improvement did not differ between physiotherapy alone and surgery at 2 years [r3] or at 6.2 years, when 8 of the physiotherapy-only shoulders had crossed over to repair; glenohumeral osteoarthritis progressed in the trial population whether or not the tear was repaired [r4]. In the Norwegian trial, differences favouring repair increased over time and were significant at 15 years (Constant score 11.8 points, pain 1.8 cm on a 10-cm scale); 15 of 51 physiotherapy patients had crossed over to surgery and unrepaired tears increased from a mean of 16.2 to 31.6 mm in the anterior–posterior direction [r6]. Untreated tears can progress: full-thickness tears enlarged more often than partial ones in MRI studies (52% versus 8% [r13]; 82.4% versus 26.1% [r14]), the review of progression found highly variable rates because definitions differed [r16], and a pooled partial-to-full-thickness progression rate of 0.26% per month was reported [r15]. Fatty infiltration and larger initial tear size predict further progression [r13,r17]. Lewis noted that outcomes of exercise may be incomplete, with persisting or recurring symptoms [r9], so a maintenance loading program is reasonable (clinical convention).
prevention: There are no trials of preventing degenerative cuff tears, and most risk factors, such as age, are not modifiable [r1]
Maintain shoulder and scapular strength and avoid long periods of deconditioning (reasonable principle; limited evidence)
Modify repetitive overhead occupational loads where possible and build load gradually after a break [r10]
Support smoking cessation and cardiovascular risk management for general health; a link to cuff tears is an association only [r10]
Seek early assessment if strength drops or night pain persists, particularly with a known full-thickness tear [r13,r14]
clinicalPearls: Do not let the scan tell the story. Cuff abnormality was found in 62% of people aged 80 or older and was similarly common whether or not they had symptoms [r1], and full-thickness tears were found in 11–17% of two population-based samples of asymptomatic shoulders [r2].

A lag sign is the finding that raises the probability of a full-thickness tear (external rotation lag LR+ 7.2, internal rotation lag LR+ 5.6, internal rotation normal LR− 0.04), whereas a painful arc just says cuff disease is likely [r18].

Exercise-first is a defensible default for gradual-onset tears: in trials of small degenerative supraspinatus tears, exercise matched surgery at 2 and 6.2 years [r3,r4], but the 15-year data and the enlarging unrepaired tears keep surgery on the table [r6]. Tell patients both.
Treat the capacity of the tendon and muscle, not the 'hole'. Degenerative regions have limited reversibility, so build load capacity in the aligned tendon through progressive loading [r12].

Full-thickness tears need follow-up: enlargement was far more frequent than for partial tears [r13,r14], and fatty infiltration or a mediolateral size of 20 mm or more flagged those at higher risk of muscle deterioration [r17].
Sudden weakness in someone with a 'known tear' is a new event until proven otherwise. Image early rather than extending an exercise trial.

animation.title: How a degenerative rotator cuff tear develops

captions.text: A 62-year-old reaches overhead repeatedly at work and around the house.
Over months to years, the load on the cuff often exceeds the capacity of an ageing tendon.
There is no single injury: the damage builds up gradually.
A minor reach or lift can make the shoulder painful and weak, though the tear was already there.
Zooming into the right shoulder, viewed from the front.

actions.text: May enlarge to full thickness over time

captions.text: The supraspinatus tendon runs under the acromion and attaches to the greater tuberosity.
Repeated load acts on a tendon with falling capacity.
The tendon becomes thickened and disorganised, with regions that no longer carry load well.
Fibres begin to fail near the footprint: a partial-thickness tear.
In some people the tear enlarges to full thickness over months to years.
The muscle can waste and fill with fat, which makes later repair or recovery harder.
Pain does not track tear size: many tears are painless and many painful tears improve with exercise.
Healthy tendon: aligned collagen with resident tenocytes.
Overload activates tenocytes and the tendon thickens. At this stage it can still recover.
With continued load the matrix breaks down and becomes disorganised.
Disorganised regions cannot carry load and have limited reversibility.
Progressive loading builds capacity in the aligned fibres, even if the disorganised area remains.
